segments.translation: [Kambalāmbarapāda]{p-kambala}, his heart delighted with the joy of supreme [compassion]{karuna}, making that same meaning plain under the guise of [compassion]{karuna}, says:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces [Kambalāmbarapāda]{p-kambala}, his heart delighted with the joy of supreme compassion, as making ‘that same meaning’ plain under the guise of compassion, the quality the song's first line gives the boat (cp.08.m1). The Tibetan has ‘the meaning of reality’ for ‘that same meaning’, and ‘the intentional language of compassion’ for ‘the guise of compassion’.

flags.note: ‘That same meaning’ translates Shastri's restored [ta]mevārthaṃ; at the head of a song it can only point back to the teaching of the earlier songs. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de kho na nyid kyi don, ‘the meaning of reality’, which may reflect tattvārtham or a similar reading rather than tam evārtham. I translated the restored Sanskrit.

karuṇāvyājena, ‘under the guise (pretext) of compassion’: the Tibetan has snying rje'i dgongs pa'i skad kyi, ‘in the intentional language of compassion’, using its usual rendering of sandhyā-bhāṣā for vyāja. The sense is close; I kept ‘guise’.
Honorific plurals (-pādāḥ … dyotayantaḥ āhuḥ) rendered as singular, as throughout.

segments.translit:
soṇetyādi karuṇeti sandhyābhāṣayā tameva bodhicittaṃ nāvīti utprekṣālaṅkāraparaṃ boddhavyaṃ| tāṃ tādātmatayā sarvvākāravaropetaśūnyatayā sadguraprasādarasaṃ [saṃ]pūryya mahāsukhacakragamanasamudroddeśenātmānaṃ saṃbodhya siddhācāryyakambalāmbarapādāvāhayanti| rūpetyādi rūpavedanāsaṃjñāsaṃskāravijñānādīnāṃ anena sthānabhedaṃ nāsti| sarvvameva tanmayatvāt| etena caturthopāyanau(no)vāhanena vinā mama siddhācāryyasya gataṃ [14ka] janmāntaraṃ vyāghuṭatītyartha| ityātmānaṃ sambodhya vadati kambalāmbarapādaḥ| nirvvikalpapravāhābhyāsaṃ kuru|
tathāca apratiṣṭhāna[pra]kāśe—
yāvān kaścit vikalpaḥ prabhavati mana[sa]styājyarūpo hi bhāvān
yo'sāvānandarūpaḥ paramasukhakaraḥ so'pi saṅkalpamātraḥ|
yo vā vairāgyabhāvastadapi tadubhayaṃ tadbhavasyāgrahetu
nirvvāṇaṃ nānyadasti kvacidapi viṣaye nirvvikalpātmacittāt||
tathāca bodhicaryyāvatāre—
mānuṣyaṃ nāvamāsādya tara duḥkhamahānadīṃ|
mūḍha kālo na nidrāyā iyannaurdurlabhā punaḥ||
segments.translation: ‘[Gold]{gold}’ and so on. ‘[Compassion]{karuna}’: in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, that same [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}; as ‘[boat]{boat}’ it is to be understood as intending the [ornament]{alankara} of [poetic fancy]{utpreksa}. Filling it, through identity with [emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects]{sarvakaravaropeta}, with the essence of the true [guru]{guru}'s grace, and addressing himself, the [siddha]{siddha} master [Kambalāmbarapāda]{p-kambala} rows it, with going to the [ocean]{ocean}, the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}, as his aim. ‘[Silver]{silver}’ (rūpā) and so on: by this there is no separate place for form (rūpa), feeling, perception, formations, [consciousness]{vijnana} and the rest, since everything is made of that. Without this rowing of the boat of the fourth means, the [birth]{janma} that has gone comes back to me, the [siddha]{siddha} master: that is the meaning. Addressing himself in this way, [Kambalāmbarapāda]{p-kambala} says: ‘Practise the flow that is free of [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}.’ As it is said in the [Apratiṣṭhānaprakāśa]{tx-apratisthanaprakasa}: ‘Whatever [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} arises from the mind is of a kind to be abandoned; the one whose form is [joy]{ananda}, that makes supreme [bliss]{sukha}, that too is mere conception; and whatever is the state of dispassion, that too: the two of them are the prime cause of that [existence]{bhava}. Nowhere among [sense objects]{visaya} is there a [nirvāṇa]{nirvana} other than one's own [mind]{citta} free of [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}.’ And as it is said in the [Bodhicaryāvatāra]{tx-bodhicaryavatara}: ‘Having found the [boat]{boat} of a human life, cross the great [river]{river} of suffering. [Fool]{mudha}, this is no time for sleep: this boat is hard to find again.’
segments.note: Munidatta reads the boat of compassion as [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, in twilight language, calling ‘boat’ a poetic figure; it is filled with the true guru's grace. He hears rūpā, ‘silver’, as rūpa, ‘form’: the aggregates have no separate place. Without rowing the boat of ‘the fourth means’, a departed birth returns; in the Tibetan, rowing it, he will not return (cp.08.m2).

equations.en: that same bodhicitta, in twilight language; calling it ‘boat’ is a poetic figure (utprekṣā)
form (rūpa), with feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, which have no separate place

citations.quoted: yāvān kaścit vikalpaḥ prabhavati manasas tyājyarūpo hi bhāvān | yo'sāv ānandarūpaḥ paramasukhakaraḥ so'pi saṅkalpamātraḥ | yo vā vairāgyabhāvas tad api tad ubhayaṃ tadbhavasyāgrahetu | nirvāṇaṃ nānyad asti kvacid api viṣaye nirvikalpātmacittāt
citations.work: Apratiṣṭhānaprakāśa (named by Munidatta; Shastri restores the syllable pra; the work is not otherwise identified here)

citations.quoted: mānuṣyaṃ nāvam āsādya tara duḥkhamahānadīm | mūḍha kālo na nidrāyā iyaṃ naur durlabhā punaḥ
citations.work: Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra, chapter 7 (on vigour), verse 14 (the work is named by Munidatta; the verse number is my identification)

flags.note: karuṇeti sandhyābhāṣayā tam eva bodhicittaṃ nāvīti … boddhavyam can be divided (a) ‘compassion’ is, in twilight language, that same bodhicitta, and calling it ‘boat’ is utprekṣā; or (b) the boat (of compassion) is, in twilight language, that same bodhicitta. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has byang chub kyi sems la gru zhes bya, ‘bodhicitta is called boat’. My English follows the word order and leaves both open; either way the boat of compassion is bodhicitta. The feminine tāṃ that follows (‘filling it’) points to nāvī, the boat.

For utprekṣālaṅkāra, ‘the ornament of poetic fancy’, the Tibetan has gzugs kyi rgyan, ‘ornament of form’, perhaps for rūpaka, ‘metaphor’, a different figure, and adds that it is to be understood ‘by others’ (gzhan la).

sadguraprasādarasaṃ [saṃ]pūryya: sadgura is evidently a slip for sadguru, and the accusative rasaṃ beside tāṃ with the absolutive saṃpūrya is awkward (perhaps originally a compound, °rasasaṃpūrṇāṃ or the like; the syllable saṃ is Shastri's restoration). The Tibetan bla ma'i drin gyi bcud kyis gang nas, ‘filled with the essence of the guru's kindness’, supports the sense I gave.

For tādātmatayā sarvākāravaropetaśūnyatayā, ‘through identity with emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects’, the Tibetan has ‘together with (lhan cig) emptiness endowed with all aspects’, without ‘supreme’.

mahāsukhacakragamanasamudroddeśena: the destination is ‘the ocean, the wheel of great bliss’, although the refrain rows ‘toward the sky’ (gaaṇa ubesem̐). Munidatta's uddeśena seems to answer the song's ubesem̐ and gamana may echo gaaṇa; he does not mention the sky. The Tibetan splits the compound: ‘…goes to the wheel of great bliss. Going on the ocean (rgya mtsho'i steng du 'gro ba) is addressing himself…’.

sarvam eva tanmayatvāt, ‘since everything is made of that’: the Tibetan has ‘since all have the nature of suchness’ (de bzhin nyid de'i rang bzhin), identifying ‘that’ as suchness, which the Sanskrit leaves unstated.

caturthopāyanau(no)vāhanena: I read caturtha-upāya-nau-vāhana, ‘rowing the boat of the fourth means’, with the manuscript's nau; Shastri's parenthesis offers no. Munidatta does not say what ‘the fourth means’ is (compare the ‘fourth instruction’ of cp.01.m6). The Tibetan bzhi pa'i thab sa la grus 'gro ba, ‘going by boat on the fourth thab sa (hearth)’, is apparently a corruption of thabs, ‘means’, and so supports upāya.

The Sanskrit says that without this rowing ‘the birth that has gone comes back’ (vyāghuṭati, a Middle Indic verb, ‘turns back’) to ‘me, the siddha master’. The Tibetan has no ‘without’ and puts it positively: ‘going by boat on the fourth means, having become a siddha master, I will not turn back in all births’ (skye ba mtha' dag tu ldog par mi 'gyur). The sense is compatible, and the Tibetan's ‘having become a siddha master’ (reading gata with siddhācārya) reads more naturally than the Sanskrit, where the failing rower calls himself siddha master; vinā may be corrupt.

In ‘addressing himself in this way, Kambalāmbarapāda says: practise the flow free of conceptual thought’, the Tibetan makes Kambalāmbarapāda the one addressed (la ba'i na bza' can gyi zhabs la), like the refrain's vocative ‘Kāmali’, and has rab tu 'bab pa, ‘flowing down’, for pravāha. I rendered pravāha ‘flow’ here and in cp.08.m3; it seems to answer the song's bāhatu, ‘row’.

Verse 1, tyājyarūpo hi bhāvān: bhāvān (accusative plural, ‘things’) does not construe; perhaps bhāvāt, ‘because it is an entity’, or a corruption (the metre, sragdharā, is intact). I left it untranslated beyond ‘is of a kind to be abandoned’. The Tibetan reads differently: ‘as long as any concept arises, the mind is to be abandoned; for so long there is duality (de srid du ni gnyis nyid phyir)’.

Verse 3, tad ubhayaṃ tadbhavasyāgrahetu: I took agrahetu as ‘prime cause’ of ‘that existence’ (tadbhava); tadbhava could also be ‘existence arising from them’. The Tibetan takes vairāgyabhāva as ‘a non-thing free of attachment’ (chags pa dang bral ba'i dngos med) and the end as ‘because of grasping it as a thing (de yi dngos por 'dzin pa'i phyir) one does not pass into nirvāṇa’, as if reading graha, ‘grasping’. Its version of line 4 is incomplete.
kvacid api viṣaye rendered ‘nowhere among sense objects’ to keep the glossary rendering of viṣaya; in this verse the phrase may mean no more than ‘in any sphere at all’.

segments.translit:
padāntareṇa tamevārthaṃ dyotayannāha—
khaṃṭītyādi| prathame khuṇṭikā ābhāṣadoṣaṃ| guruvā[e]kya dṛḍhīkṛtya utpāṭya(dya) bho yogivara| kacchikāsu vidyāsūtrañca muktīkṛtya drutaṃ tasyāḥ pravāhaṃ kuru| etenābhāṣaviśeṣeṇa anuttaradharmmasākṣātvāṭikācitto(tve) hi bhavatīti nātra saṃśayaḥ|
segments.translation: Making that same meaning plain with another [verse]{pada}, he says: ‘[Stake]{khunti}’ and so on. First, the [stake]{khunti}: the fault of [appearance]{abhasa}. Having made the [guru]{guru}'s word firm, pull it up, O best of [yogis]{yogi}; and having loosened the thread of [knowledge]{vidya} in the [ropes]{kacchi}, swiftly set it flowing. Through this particular [appearance]{abhasa} one comes to realize the [unsurpassed]{anuttara} [Dharma]{dharma} directly; of this there is no doubt.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the stake as the fault of [appearance]{abhasa}, which the best of yogis pulls up once he has made the guru's word firm; loosening a ‘thread of knowledge’ in the ropes, he sets it flowing swiftly and so realizes the unsurpassed Dharma. The Tibetan has ‘thread of ignorance’, and the guru's word producing firmness rather than uprooting (cp.08.m3).

equations.en: the fault of appearance (ābhāsadoṣa), to be pulled up once the guru's word is made firm
a thread of knowledge (vidyāsūtra) in the ropes, to be loosened; the Tibetan has ‘the thread of ignorance’

flags.note: utpāṭya(dya): I translated utpāṭya, ‘having pulled up’, which matches the song's upāṛī. Shastri's parenthesis offers utpādya, ‘having produced’, and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) supports it: dang po la snang ba'i nyes pa la bla ma'i gsung gis brtan pa skyed par byed do, ‘first, against the fault of appearance, the guru's word produces firmness’, with no uprooting.

kacchikāsu vidyāsūtrañ ca, ‘and the thread of knowledge in the ropes’: the Tibetan has nyag thag ni ma rig pa'i srad bu, ‘the rope is the thread of ignorance’, which makes better sense of loosening it. The written Sanskrit cannot distinguish kacchikā + avidyā° from kacchikā vidyā° once sandhi is applied, so the Sanskrit's ‘knowledge’ may be a misdivision; the locative plural kacchikāsu is also odd. I translated the Sanskrit as printed.

anuttaradharmasākṣātvāṭikācitto(tve) is corrupt (vāṭikā, ‘garden’, makes no sense here; Shastri's (tve) suggests an abstract noun). I translated by the sense of the Tibetan, bla na med pa'i chos mngon sum du byed par 'gyur, ‘comes to make the unsurpassed Dharma manifest’, which points to sākṣātkāritve or sākṣātkārī.
guruvā[e]kya: Shastri's bracketed vowel sign is unclear; read guruvākyaṃ, ‘the guru's word’, as the Tibetan bla ma'i gsung confirms.

etenābhāsaviśeṣeṇa, ‘through this particular appearance’, might also be ‘through this distinction of appearance’; the Tibetan has de rnams kyi snang ba'i khyad par gyis, ‘through the distinction of their appearance’ (plural). ‘Set it flowing’ renders tasyāḥ pravāhaṃ kuru; the feminine tasyāḥ presumably refers to the boat (nāvī).

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena gurorasampradāyāt viparyyayamāha—
māṅgatetyādi| mārgaṃ viramānandaṃ gatvā caturdiśaṃ grāhyādi vi[15]na[ā] saṃsāre patati|
tathāca caryyāpādaḥ—
khālata paṛilem̐ kāpura nāśai| iti|
yaḥ punaḥ sadguruvacanena pavipaṅkajasukhānveṣaṇaṃ karoti sa bhavajaladhau pāraṃ gacchatīti|
tathāca kṛṣṇācāryyapādāḥ—
jo saṃveaṇa maṇaraaṇa
aharaha sahaja pharanta|
so para jānai dharmmagai
anu kimu naa kahanta||
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he speaks of the error that comes from lacking the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}: ‘[Māṅga]{manga}’ and so on. Having gone onto the path, the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, and looking in the four directions at the grasped and the rest, without … he falls into [saṃsāra]{samsara}. As a line of a song of [conduct]{carya} says: ‘When camphor falls into a ditch, it is lost.’ But one who, by the true [guru]{guru}'s word, seeks the [bliss]{sukha} of [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus} goes [across]{para} the [ocean]{ocean} of [existence]{bhava}. As [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} says: ‘One whose mind-[jewel]{ratna} of self-experience radiates the [innate]{sahaja} day after day, he alone knows the way of [dharma]{dharma}. What else can others say?’
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as the error of one lacking the guru's lineage: the [māṅga]{manga} is the path, the joy of cessation; whoever goes onto it and looks at the grasped and the rest falls into saṃsāra. The Sanskrit is broken here; in the Tibetan, lacking the guru's word as boatman, he cannot reach the wheel of great bliss (cp.08.m4).

equations.en: the path (mārga), the joy of cessation

citations.work: an unidentified caryā song; the Sanskrit says only caryāpāda, ‘a line of a caryā’, while the Tibetan attributes it to Kṛṣṇācārya's song (nag po spyod pa'i glu dbyangs)

citations.quoted: jo saṃveaṇa maṇaraaṇa | aharaha sahaja pharanta | so para jānai dharmagai | anu kimu naa kahanta
citations.work: a dohā of Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha), whom Munidatta names as its author; perhaps from Kāṇha's Dohākoṣa, which he does not name here

flags.note: The Sanskrit is lacunose at the folio change (vi[15]na[ā], ‘without’, is left with no object), marked by an ellipsis. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has the full sentence: ‘having gone on the path of the joy of cessation, if he looks at and examines the concepts of grasped and grasper and so on in the four directions, then, lacking the mnyen pa of the guru's word, he cannot go to the wheel of great bliss, travelled by the nature of innate joy, and certainly falls again into saṃsāra’. mnyen pa appears to be mnyan pa, ‘boatman’; the Tibetan song line 4b uses the same word (gru skya med par mnyen pa gang gis 'gro).
The Sanskrit gives only accusatives (caturdiśaṃ grāhyādi); I supplied ‘looking at’ from the song's cāhaa, ‘looks’, which the Tibetan also has (lta zhing rtog par byed na, ‘if he looks and examines’).

caryāpādaḥ (singular) most naturally means ‘a line (pāda) of a caryā’; I translated it so. The Tibetan attributes the line to ‘the song of Kṛṣṇācārya’ (nag po spyod pa'i glu dbyangs), and the glossary records spyod pa'i zhabs, ‘Caryāpāda’, as a Tibetan form of Kāṇha's name, so the Sanskrit may have lost kṛṣṇa- or mean a person. I have not found the line in the songs in the pack. The Tibetan has dong, ‘pit’, for khāla, ‘ditch’.

The dohā's last line, anu kimu naa kahanta, is obscure. I took anu as anya, ‘others’, and the line as a rhetorical question. Alternatives: naa as naya, ‘what other way do they teach?’; or with naa as the negative, ‘what do others not say?’. The Tibetan has thub pa rnams kyis gzhan du ci zhig gsungs, ‘what else have the sages said?’, as if reading muni.

In the dohā the Tibetan has phug pas, ‘by piercing’, where the Apabhraṃśa has saṃveaṇa (saṃvedana, ‘self-experience’), perhaps reading saṃvedhana; and chos kyi gnas, ‘the place of dharma’, for dharmagai (dharmagati, ‘the way of dharma’).

pavi, Indra's thunderbolt, stands for vajra in pavipaṅkaja, ‘vajra and lotus’; the Tibetan has rdo rje dang chu skyes. The Tibetan quotes the song's word as gru'i mjug, ‘stern’, but glosses it, like the Sanskrit, as the path, and renders viramānanda here dga' bral.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena phalavyaktīkaraṇamāha—
vāmadāhiṇetyādi| vāmadakṣiṇamābhāsadvayaṃ madhyamāyāṃ praveśayitvā| mārgaviramānandagataṃ bodhicittaṃ nijajñānapariśodhitaṃ| mahāsukhacakrasamudroddeśena yadā militaṃ tasmin mārge mahāsukhasaṅganairātmājñānābhisaṃgaṃ mayā prāptamiti| 8||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks of making the fruit manifest: ‘[Left and right]{vama-daksina}’ and so on. ‘Having made the pair of [appearances]{abhasa}, [left and right]{vama-daksina}, enter the [central channel]{madhyama}, when [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, gone to the path, the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, and purified by one's own knowledge, has met, with the [ocean]{ocean}, the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}, as its goal, then on that path I have obtained the embrace of the knowledge of [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, the [companion]{companion} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}.’
segments.note: Munidatta reads the last couplet as the fruit: left and right are the two appearances, made to enter the central channel; [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, on the path of the joy of cessation and purified by one's own knowledge, meets the ocean, the wheel of great bliss, and the poet obtains the embrace of the knowledge of Nairātmā, companion of great bliss (cp.08.m5).

equations.en: the pair of appearances, left and right, made to enter the central channel
the path, the joy of cessation, to which bodhicitta has gone
the knowledge of Nairātmā, the companion of great bliss, whose embrace the poet obtains

flags.note: For mārgaviramānandagataṃ, ‘gone to the path, the joy of cessation’, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has lam sna tshogs pa'i dga' bar gyur pa, ‘the path become the joy of variety’; in cp.08.m4 it renders the same Sanskrit word dga' bral. It also has ‘having purified one's own knowledge’ (rang gi ye shes yongs su sbyangs nas) where the Sanskrit has bodhicitta ‘purified by one's own knowledge’, and ‘the knowledge of selflessness’ (bdag med pa'i ye shes) for nairātmājñāna, with no goddess.
The Tibetan quotes the couplet's opening as byang dang lho, ‘north and south’ (as in its song line 5a), and glosses it as left and right (g.yon dang g.yas), which fits an observer facing east.

The paraphrase is in the poet's first person (mayā prāptam, ‘I have obtained’), closed by iti; I set it in quotation marks. Munidatta's militaṃ and saṅga echo the song's milila and sa(su)ṅgā. The closing ‘8’ is the song number and is not translated.

proposals.definition: The ocean or sea (Sanskrit samudra, jaladhi; Tibetan rgya mtsho). The songs speak of rivers, but Munidatta often speaks of an ocean: in song 8 the boat goes to ‘the ocean, the wheel of great bliss’ (cp.08.m2, cp.08.m5), and whoever seeks bliss by the true guru's word crosses the ocean of existence (cp.08.m4).
proposals.symbolicImage: an ocean, which the boat goes to or crosses

symbolicReadings.referent: the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukhacakra), named in apposition as the ocean the boat goes to; the song itself rows toward the sky
existence (bhava): the ocean of existence, crossed by one who seeks the bliss of vajra and lotus by the true guru's word

proposals.rationale: Munidatta's recurring image for the boat's goal and for saṃsāra. It is not in the lines of song 8, but it occurs three times in this commentary, and existing entries record the ocean of saṃsāra in his comments on songs 5 and 14 (moksa, para). An entry lets the woven commentary link it consistently.

questions: The alankara entry (‘ornament’) is defined as a yogi's regalia. In cp.08.m2 alaṅkāra is the term of Sanskrit poetics, a figure of speech (utprekṣālaṅkāra). I used ‘ornament’ as the entry requires; should the entry be widened to cover the poetics sense, or should a separate term (e.g. ‘figure of speech’) be created?

p-kanha has the English ‘Kāṇha’. Munidatta's Sanskrit in cp.08.m4 names him Kṛṣṇācāryapāda. I used [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} as the glossary requires. Should commentary translations keep his Sanskrit name, Kṛṣṇācārya, as a variant?

cp.08.m3: the Sanskrit has ‘thread of knowledge’ (vidyāsūtra), the Tibetan ‘thread of ignorance’ (ma rig pa'i srad bu). The sandhi could hide avidyā°. I translated the Sanskrit as printed. Do you want the English to follow the Tibetan here, with a note?

cp.08.m3: the phrase ending in sākṣātvāṭikācitto(tve) is corrupt; I translated it by the sense of the Tibetan (‘comes to realize the unsurpassed Dharma directly’). Is that acceptable, or should the English mark the corruption?

cp.08.m4: I marked the lacuna at the folio change with an ellipsis rather than filling it from the Tibetan, which there has the guru's word as ‘boatman’ (mnyen pa, apparently for mnyan pa) and the failure to reach the wheel of great bliss. Should the gap be filled from the Tibetan in the translation or left to the note and flag? Please also check mnyen pa as ‘boatman’.

cp.08.m2: to make Munidatta's pun visible I kept rūpā and rūpa in parentheses in the commentary translation (‘Silver (rūpā) … form (rūpa)’). Is this acceptable in woven commentary, or should the pun be left to the note?
cp.08.m2: Munidatta's ‘the fourth means’ (caturthopāya) is unexplained. Is it the ‘fourth instruction’ of cp.01.m6, the fourth empowerment, or something else? I left it literal.
I proposed a new entry ‘ocean’ (samudra, jaladhi, rgya mtsho), which recurs in this commentary as the boat's goal and as the ocean of existence. Keep it, or leave ocean unlinked?

For the draft line cp.08.2a (reference only, not changed): Munidatta's paraphrase (cp.08.m2) has ‘with going to the ocean, the wheel of great bliss, as his aim’, where uddeśena seems to answer ubesem̐; the Tibetan song line has ‘having looked at the sky’ (nam mkha' bltas nas). ‘Toward the sky’ fits Munidatta's reading of ubesem̐; you may want a witness note on the Tibetan.
